problem: Existing ObjectNav/ZSON datasets are static, lack dynamic (moving human) obstacles, uncommon open-vocabulary goal objects, same-category objects with distinct spatial/appearance attributes, and scene text hints. They also only check collisions with static obstacles.
motivation: Real homes contain moving people, diverse and uncommon objects, multiple instances of a category, and text notes. ZSON methods evaluated on static, closed-vocabulary ObjectNav data therefore cannot be assessed for safety, fine-grained recognition or multimodal reasoning.
key_idea: Build DOZE, an AI2-THOR-based dataset of ten scenes and 18k+ tasks with static and dynamic humanoid obstacles, open-vocabulary and distinct-attribute goals, and hint whiteboards, plus a humanoid collision-detection interface and a Collision Rate metric.
insight: All four baselines are weak on DOZE (Level 1 SR about 22-25% average), and SPL falls while CR rises from Level 1 to Level 3 for every method. Dynamic humanoids break map-based methods: C-L3MVN's semantic map models moving people as continuous obstacles and stalls exploration. The mapless C-LGX is weaker overall. The ablation shows that removing the other object types from the scenes raises SR (e.g. OV 12.5→14.6), so each object type adds difficulty. Hint use (OCR+LLM intermediate goal) gives large SPL gains (L3MVN 9.1→13.3 at Level 1).
method: Humanoid obstacles: three levels: L1 static humanoids occluding goals, L2 dynamic humanoids on fixed paths with pauses, L3 dynamic humanoids walking to random points
Open-vocabulary objects: free 3D models plus text-to-3D generation (ProlificDreamer, DreamFusion) add new categories and objects with rich properties
Distinct-attribute objects: same-category instances differ in spatial relations (pillow on sofa) or appearance (color, material, texture, brand)
Hint objects: whiteboards with text notes point to a location of the goal object, with an intermediate goal such as a bed
Collision interface and metric: collision if the agent is within 0.2 m of a humanoid; CR = mean over episodes of collisions/steps; Humanoid Density metric
Baselines: Random, Frontier, C-L3MVN (LLM frontier selection with humanoid-aware semantic map), C-LGX (GLIP+LLM, predicts humanoid motion from two steps)
Hint-informed methods H-Frontier/H-L3MVN: OCR reads the whiteboard, an LLM combines it with the goal to give an intermediate target, then the agent rotates and searches around it

setting.backbone: Frontier exploration; L3MVN (LLM + semantic map, C-L3MVN); LGX (GLIP/BLIP + LLM, C-LGX); OCR + LLM for hints
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + agent pose + goal category

numbers_note: DOZE has no official splits. Since the paper reports no split names, 'test' is used. Only selected baseline rows are listed, since these are the paper's own adapted variants (C-L3MVN, C-LGX, H-L3MVN); the full 9-column table is in Table 2. The ablation (Table 3) gives C-L3MVN SR/SPL with target-type objects only: OV 14.6/4.2, Spatial 26.5/7.7, Appearance 35.5/9.7. The paper's ablation table row for 'all types' (12.5/3.8, 23.8/7.0, 32.8/9.2) does not match Table 2 for C-L3MVN (it matches the C-LGX row values).
results: On DOZE all methods perform poorly. C-L3MVN is the best on Level 1 (average SR 24.7%), above Frontier and C-LGX (22.3%). SPL drops and CR rises from Level 1 to Level 3 for all methods (Level 3 CR about 11-20% versus <1% at Level 1). Hint-informed H-L3MVN beats L3MVN in SR and SPL at all levels (Level 1 SPL 13.3 vs 9.1).
limitations: Small scale: 10 scenes (AI2-THOR) and only 34 hint tasks per level; small hint evaluation (SR granularity ~3%)
Only four simple baselines adapted by the authors, without strong dedicated dynamic-obstacle methods; humanoids are simulated
Simulator-only, indoor-only; the ablation table appears inconsistent with the main table
